data.title: HTTP Status Code
data.tagline: A three-digit answer from the server about a request: success, redirect, a request problem, or a server failure
data.learningOutcome: You can read what a status code category means and decide whether to check the frontend, the deployment, the request, or the server.
data.description: When a page fails, a 404 response says the target resource was not found; check the URL, route, and deployment. A 500 is a server-error-class response; correlate its request ID with server logs to find clues. A status code points to the next check but does not prove the root cause or responsibility on its own.

learning.assumes: You have seen a page fail to open, an error, or a form that does nothing.
learning.outcome: You can read what a status code category means and decide whether to check the frontend, the deployment, the request, or the server.

distinctions.label: On-page error text
distinctions.explanation: Text like loading failed is decided by frontend code and may appear regardless of the response. The status code comes from the server and is the more reliable first piece of evidence.

distinctions.label: HTTP method
distinctions.explanation: The method says what the request intends to do; the status code says what the response reported. A resource can return 405 when a method is disallowed, but a wrong method can also produce another response.

explanation.title: Read the category first
explanation.text: The first digit groups response classes: 2xx success, 3xx redirection, 4xx client error, and 5xx server error. This guides the next check; use the request and logs to locate a cause.

explanation.title: The exact number narrows the cause
explanation.text: A 404 response says the target resource was not found, 401 means valid authentication credentials are missing, and 400 signals a problem with the request. Check the URL, request, and response for the cause.

explanation.title: Where to find it
explanation.text: The browser Network panel records the status code of every request; debugging tools and errors reported by AI agents also print the number directly.

data.boundary: A status code describes the request outcome, not whether the code has bugs. A 200 also does not prove the business result: a save endpoint can return success while nothing was written, so acceptance still depends on the business outcome.

lessonPractice.title: A form shows a generic network error, and the Network panel reports 500. What should happen first?

options.label: Treat 500 as a server-side failure and check server logs for this request
options.feedback: 500 is a server-error-class response. Correlate its request ID with server logs; the status alone does not locate the root cause. Page text cannot replace that evidence.

options.label: Retry repeatedly because the page message says network error
options.feedback: 500 means the responding side reported a server error; check correlated logs to see whether the request reached your application and what failed. Retrying can hide clues.

options.label: Inspect frontend code first because the page renders the message
options.feedback: The page decides what text to show; a 500 is a server-error-class response, so check the correlated request in server logs next.

data.agentPrompt: The page returns 404 and the form returns 500. Check each URL, status, and response in Network; review the route or deployment for the 404, and correlate the 500 request ID with server logs. After fixing it, resend and verify the page and saved data.
